name: Sugaring paste

lead: Sugaring paste is a sugar-based substance spread on skin and pulled off to remove hair at the root. Fans prefer it to wax because it is water-soluble and can be used at lower temperatures.
It is a temporary method like other epilation. Claims of less pain and fewer broken hairs are widespread but have not been tested in published comparisons.

paras: The paste adheres to hair and is flicked or stripped off, pulling hairs out with their roots.
Skin irritation is possible, especially on sensitive skin. Reviews note limited evidence on risks and that studies mostly cover dark hair and fair skin.

lead: Sugaring paste is a sticky mixture, traditionally of sugar, water and lemon juice, applied to the skin and removed to pull out hair, and is marketed as an alternative to wax [1]. Sugaring is classed in the medical literature as a form of epilation, grouped with plucking, threading, waxing, lasers and electrolysis [2].

Proponents say the paste grips hair rather than skin, is water-soluble and can be used at room temperature or lightly warmed [1]. Sugaring is also reported as one of the methods used for pubic hair removal [3]. The published literature contains reviews of hair removal generally but no trials that specifically compare sugaring with waxing.
infobox: Sugar, water, lemon juice; sometimes honey, cornstarch [1]
Reported as hair ready again after 8 to 10 days [1]

paras: Home recipes typically combine sugar, water and lemon juice, with cornstarch, honey or molasses in some versions; the acid in the lemon breaks sucrose down into simpler sugars, yielding a smooth non-crystalline paste [1]. Commercial pastes may add guar gum or essential oils, and some products sold as sugar waxes contain actual wax [1].

In the strip method the skin is dusted with powder, paste is spread on, and a cloth or paper strip is pressed in and pulled off along the direction of hair growth. In the traditional hand method the paste is applied against hair growth and flicked off with it, without strips, and residue is rinsed away with water [1].
Wikipedia states the method dates to about 1900 BC and was long confined to the Persian region; honey is thought to have been the earliest sugaring agent [1].

Proponents report less pain than waxing, easier cleanup, and a shorter wait between sessions [1]. These claims are not backed by cited trials in the available sources. A literature review found that most studies of hair removal methods are restricted to darker hair and fairer skin and that all methods besides electrolysis are temporary, each with its own advantages and adverse events [2].

Irritation or reaction on sensitive skin can occur [1]. A dermatological review of genital hair removal found little evidence on risks for methods such as sugaring and noted that there is no medical indication for it in most cases [3].
No studies found specific to sugaring paste. Broader reviews of hair removal practices list sugaring among epilation methods without separate efficacy data [2][3].
